big_idea: If more comes in, we add. If some leaves, we subtract. Stories tell us which one.
learning_intention: We are learning to listen to a snack-shop story, decide if we add or subtract, and find the answer with cubes.
student_learning_goal: I can listen to a snack-shop story, act it out with cubes, and tell how many are altogether or how many are left.
success_criteria: I can show the start of the story with cubes.
I can decide if I add or take away based on the story.
I can write the answer as a number sentence.
lesson_specific_materials: 8 'Snack Shop Story' picture cards (teacher-prepared) showing pennies, popcorn, lollipops, cookies
Anchor chart 'When do we ADD? When do we TAKE AWAY?' with two columns ready for student-generated examples

OPTIONAL: Penny and Nick — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 3 formative tracker (Operation Choice) — provided in assessment_suite stage
Mid-unit formative worksheet 'Numerals 0–10 Check-In' (provided in formative_reflection stage)

minds_on.hook: A customer walks up to Penny's snack shop with a problem — and the answer is hiding inside a story.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Hold up Penny and a small pile of 7 pennies.

'Friends — Penny opened the snack shop today. A customer came in. Listen carefully and you'll see the math hiding inside the story.' Read slowly: 'Penny had SEVEN pennies in her pocket. A customer paid her THREE more. How many pennies does Penny have ALTOGETHER?'

Hold up your finger. 'Watch what I do with the cubes.' Build a tower of 7 (red); add 3 more (yellow). 'Seven AND three. The story said MORE came in — so we add.' Count the new tower. 'Ten altogether.' Write 7 + 3 = 10 on the chart under the ADD column.

Now tell a take-away story: 'Penny had 10 cubes. Nick took 4 to deliver to the carpet customers. How many are LEFT?' Pull 4 cubes off the tower. 'Ten take away four. SIX are left.' Add 10 − 4 = 6 to the chart's TAKE AWAY column. 'Today we are going to listen to lots of stories. Your job: decide — do we add, or do we take away? The story tells us.'

Penny's refrain. Class chants 3x with claps: 'STORY first — SIGN next — COUNT last! That's how Penny shops!'
student_actions: Listen to each story without speaking.
Watch the cube model and count along.
Decide aloud: 'add' or 'take away' after each story.

action.activity_name: Listen, Act, Solve — Whole Group then Stations

steps.instruction: Whole group: read three more stories together. After each, ask the class to vote with thumbs (add up vs add down) before modelling with cubes. Story A: 'Nick had 5 cubes; he found 4 more.' Story B: 'Penny baked 8 cookies; the dog ate 2.' Story C: 'Quincy had 6 pennies; Penny put 3 more in the slot.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Listen first. Don't shout. THUMBS up if it's an ADD story. THUMBS down if it's a TAKE AWAY story.' Read each story slowly twice. After thumb vote, build with cubes. Discuss the keyword that gave it away ('found' = add, 'ate' = take away, 'put more in' = add).

steps.instruction: Build the keyword chart together. List on the anchor chart: ADD words (more, found, gave, came, altogether) vs TAKE AWAY words (ate, gone, left, took, less). Children volunteer extra words from their own experience.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'What words tell us to ADD? What words tell us to TAKE AWAY?' Add their words to the chart. Don't accept words that don't pass the test — for any word a child suggests, ask 'in our story would more come in or some go away?' Confirm before writing.

steps.instruction: Send children to three rotating stations: (a) Cube Station with picture-card stories and snap-cubes; (b) Coin Station with picture-card stories and real Canadian pennies; (c) Ten-Frame Station with the same stories solved on the M4 mat. Each station has 2–3 stories from the 8-card teacher-prepared set; pairs work together.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You'll work in pairs at three stations. At each station, read your picture card together, decide ADD or TAKE AWAY, and solve with the materials at that station. Switch when you hear the chime.' 8-min rotations × 3.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: After station rotation, gather the class. Pick two pairs who solved the SAME story problem at different stations (one with cubes, one with the ten-frame). Each pair shares — same story, two ways. Class debates: did the answer match? (Yes.) Which way felt fastest? Which way would you pick if you were on your own? Make the point: 'Different tools, same answer. Same story tells the same operation.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Two pairs, one story, two ways. Watch.' After both share, pose 'pick a tool' for the next round. Affirm both, but flag that the OPERATION (add/take away) is the same regardless of tool.

steps.instruction: Mid-unit formative check (after Lesson 3 only): hand out the 3-prompt 'Numerals 0–10 Check-In' worksheet. Children complete it independently while the teacher circulates with the formative tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You're going to do a quick check on your own — three story problems. Take your time. Build with cubes if you need to.' Walk around. For each child, record on the tracker whether they (a) chose the right operation, (b) modelled correctly, (c) wrote the right answer.

differentiation.for_emerging: These children stay at the Cube Station for all three rotations and skip the Coin/Ten-Frame stations. The cube model is concrete enough that they can keep up. Use story cards limited to totals ≤ 5 for emerging children (recycle the partners-of-5 from Lesson 2).
differentiation.for_extending: Two-step stretch cards available at each station: 'Penny had 4 pennies. Nick gave her 3 more, then a customer paid 2. How many altogether?' Stays inside A6.12 (situations to 10) but adds a chained operation.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a visual 'add or take away?' card with arrows and a scale icon. The child can point to the icon rather than say the word. Picture cards have minimal text; stories are narrated.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: NO-PAPER, NO-CUBE PATH: Acted-out story corners. Carpet has TWO corners — ADD corner and TAKE-AWAY corner. Teacher reads stories aloud. Children walk to the matching corner. Then in the corner, children act out the math with their bodies — 5 children stand for the start, 3 more walk in (add) or 2 walk out (take away). Whole lesson runs on bodies + class voice; story cards optional, teacher can read instead. No purchased cubes/coins/ten-frames required.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Does the child choose the right operation for each story? Does the cube/coin/ten-frame model match the story? Can they articulate the keyword that signalled add vs take away? Mid-unit worksheet captures this on paper.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick each child's column on the tracker per station. The mid-unit worksheet has 3 prompts; record the per-prompt result.
tracker_columns: Models the start of the story with materials
Writes the answer as a number sentence

discussion_prompts: When you were at the stations, what was a word that told you to ADD?
What was a word that told you to TAKE AWAY?
Penny had 4 cubes and Nick took 1. Tell me what that story sounds like in your own words. How many are left?
Can you tell us your OWN snack-shop story? Tell us the start, what changed, and the end.
consolidation.exit_routine: Refrain chant 3x. Then each child whispers one snack-shop story to their carpet partner. The partner says ADD or TAKE AWAY. Partners switch. Pull two children to share their story with the whole class as a model.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Operation Choice tracker (per-station observation) for A6.12, plus the 3-prompt Numerals 0–10 Check-In worksheet.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: A6.12 is the keystone expectation: situations to 10 require both choosing the right operation AND executing it with materials. The mid-unit check pinpoints which children need extra practice on operation choice (vs. computation) before Day 4. Children who get the right ANSWER but the wrong OPERATION are flagged for Day 4 small-group review.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child solves the math but picks the wrong operation — repairing operation choice for A6.12 (Carpenter & Moser CGI, 1983; Riley & Greeno, 1988; Fuson, 1992)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On A6.12, the most-documented K trap is the child who can compute (7+3=10; 10−4=6) but cannot LISTEN to a story and decide which operation models it.

Carpenter & Moser's (1983) Cognitively Guided Instruction (CGI) work classifies K-grade addition/subtraction situations into a six-cell taxonomy: Join Result-Unknown ('Penny had 7, got 3 more, has __'), Join Change-Unknown ('Penny had 7, got some more, now has 10 — got __ more'), Join Start-Unknown, Separate Result-Unknown ('Penny had 10, gave 4 away, has __'), Separate Change-Unknown, Separate Start-Unknown. K children typically master ONLY Join Result-Unknown and Separate Result-Unknown — the two simplest cells. This lesson stays inside those two cells deliberately, but exposes the child who is doing 'numeric pattern-match' rather than 'situation modelling'.

Riley & Greeno (1988) showed empirically that K-G1 children's success on word problems depends overwhelmingly on the SCHEMA they recognise (join vs separate), not on the numbers. A child who 'computes correctly but writes the wrong sign' has done numeric pattern-match without schema recognition — they saw 6 and 3, returned 9, and assigned a sign at random. Riley & Greeno call this 'direct modelling without semantic structure'.

Fuson (1992) traces the development of word-problem strategies: K children move from direct-modelling (act it out with cubes), through counting-strategies (count-on for join), to part-part-whole derived facts. The keyword chart in Step 2 is a transitional scaffold from direct modelling toward schema recognition.

Why this matters: the entire rest of the unit, especially Day 5's Snack Shop, assumes the child can map a story to an operation. Step 4 (mid-unit formative) is the gate. A child who can compute but can't choose the right operation will FAIL Grade 1 word problems within months — repair must happen now.

The walkthrough covers the child whose answer is mathematically right but operationally wrong.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Mid-unit formative worksheet is in front of the child. Prompt 1 reads: 'Penny had 6 pennies. A customer gave her 3 more. How many altogether?' The child has correctly written 9 — but they wrote 6 − 3 = 9 instead of 6 + 3 = 9. The answer is right; the operation is wrong. They are about to flip the page. The teacher steps in BEFORE they move on.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. Don't correct yet. 'Tell me about your answer.' Wait. They'll usually say 'nine!' confidently. 'How did you get nine? Walk me through it.' They may say 'I added 6 and 3' even though their writing shows minus. The mismatch is the diagnosis.

'Look at what you wrote here.' Point to the minus sign. 'You wrote 6 take away 3. But the customer GAVE Penny more pennies. Did Penny end up with MORE or LESS?' Wait. (More.) 'When she ends up with MORE, do we add or take away?' (Add.) 'Right. So this should be …' Let them say plus. Hand them an eraser; they fix the sign.

The critical follow-up: 'How did you get the right answer if you used the wrong sign?' Most children will say 'I just counted in my head.' Affirm, but redirect: 'Your counting was good. But sometimes the numbers don't tell us which sign — the STORY does. Listen to the story first. Then write the sign. Then count.' Watch them finish prompts 2 and 3. If both are operationally correct, tick the 'connects story to operation' column. If they slip again, pair them for Day 4 small-group review with the keyword chart in front of them.

A6.12 isn't really about the answer — it's about the modelling. A child who can compute but can't choose the right operation will FAIL Grade 1 word problems within months. The repair must happen now.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Picks an operation at random (often whichever symbol they wrote first), gets the right answer by happenstance counting, doesn't notice the symbol mismatch.
(Mid) Hesitates between + and −, looks at the story for cues, gets it right after re-reading. Operation choice is conscious but not automatic.
(Strong) Reads the story, points to the keyword ('GAVE' = add), writes the equation, computes. The whole flow is fluent.
(Stretched) Explains aloud: 'I see GAVE so I write plus. If it had said TOOK I would write minus.' Has internalised the keyword-to-operation map.
common_misconceptions: The numbers in the story tell us the operation. (Some children look at the order — 'big number minus small number' — without listening to what's happening. The story matters more than the numbers.)
Plus and minus are interchangeable as long as you get the right answer. (A child who computes correctly but writes the wrong sign has not yet separated the two operations conceptually.)
Take-away always means the bigger number minus the smaller. (Some take-away stories don't have an obvious bigger number. The repair is to model the START with cubes BEFORE deciding.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child writes wrong sign but correct answer (Riley & Greeno 1988 'direct modelling without semantic structure' — pattern-matched the numbers): replay the story; child must point to the keyword (GAVE, ATE, FOUND, TOOK) BEFORE writing any sign; if the keyword is on the ADD column, write +; if on the TAKE-AWAY column, write −. Sign comes from the chart, not the numbers. Repeat for the next 3 stories before letting them work alone.

DIAGNOSTIC B — child mis-models the START (uses wrong starting number, e.g., starts with 3 instead of 7): always have the child PHYSICALLY BUILD the starting number with cubes BEFORE deciding the operation. The cube-action of the story (more cubes added, or cubes removed) makes the operation choice physical. Direct-modelling is Fuson's (1992) entry stage — most stable for K — and CGI children only progress past it when they're already fluent at it.

DIAGNOSTIC C — child cannot identify the keyword in the story (operation-choice fails because the schema cue is missed): use the two-corner body-trace. Read the story aloud; child stands and walks to the ADD corner or the TAKE-AWAY corner of the carpet; THEN names which keyword pulled them there. Embodied schema recognition: walking the schema in space is a reliable bridge to verbal labelling for K children.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of A6.12 — listening to (or reading) a story, choosing the operation, modelling with cubes or coins, and writing the equation.

parts_outline.task: Three illustrated story problems (one add, one take away, one add). Each has a picture, a 1–2 sentence narrative, and a blank equation line. The child writes the operation and the answer.
Two stories where the child must DRAW their model. Story 1: 'Penny had 4 cubes; Nick gave her 3 more.' Story 2: 'Quincy had 9 pennies; Nick took 5.' Empty boxes labelled START / CHANGE / END.
Story-builder grid: a target equation (e.g. 6 − 2 = 4) is given. The child writes their own snack-shop story that matches it. Sentence starters scaffold the writing.
